---
title: "EU FDI screening notifications jumped 40% in 2025, and 12% of deals now face in-depth review"
slug: eu-fdi-screening-notification-surge-2026
category: trade-policy
audience: importer
keyword: "EU FDI screening notification 2025 in-depth assessment importer investor"
description: "Notifications to the EU's FDI cooperation mechanism rose 40% between 2024 and 2025, to 667 deals, and 12% went to in-depth security review. What that means for an importer or investor planning an EU stake."
date: 2026-10-18
sources:
  - "European Commission, Directorate-General for Trade and Economic Security — 'Screening of foreign direct investment continues to advance EU security and public order', 14 October 2026"
  - "Sixth Annual Report on the Screening of FDI into the EU (referenced in the Commission news article)"
---

## The number that matters if you are buying into Europe

If you are an importer or an investor planning an acquisition or a greenfield stake in the EU, the
Commission's sixth annual FDI screening report gives you two figures to plan around: a 15-day window
that most deals clear, and a 12% chance that yours does not.

Notifications to the EU's cooperation mechanism increased by 40% between 2024 and 2025. In absolute
terms, EU Member States notified 667 investments to the Commission in 2025, up from 477 notifications
in 2024.

## Most deals clear in 15 days — but not all

Of the 667 cases notified, 88% were closed within 15 days. That is the base case for a straightforward
deal: a notification, a short clock, and a clearance.

The remaining 12% of the investments notified to the Commission required an in-depth security risk
assessment — a 4% rise compared to last year. That is the tail you have to budget for, because an
in-depth assessment is not a 15-day event.

## Where the in-depth cases land

Most such cases were in manufacturing, which accounted for 53% of all transactions, up from 50% in
2024. If your target sits in manufacturing, the in-depth review is not a remote risk; it is the
sector where the Commission's own reporting says the reviews concentrate.

## The regime you will actually be filing under

The EU's new Foreign Investment Screening Regulation (FISR) was adopted on 17 June 2026 and will apply
from 17 January 2028. Deals notified before that date run under the current cooperation mechanism
described above. Deals notified after it run under FISR.

## What to do with these figures

Three planning consequences follow directly from the numbers above, and no others:

1. **Price the 15-day clock as the base case, not the guarantee.** 88% of notified cases closed inside
   15 days in 2025. Build your completion timetable around the 12% that did not.
2. **Treat manufacturing targets as the in-depth case until told otherwise.** Manufacturing was 53% of
   all transactions in the notified population, and the Commission reports that most in-depth cases
   were there.
3. **Check your notification date against 17 January 2028.** A deal that slips past that date is
   assessed under a different regulation than one that does not.

## What this article does not tell you

The directive behind this piece carries seven figures, all from the Commission's 14 October 2026
release and the sixth annual report it describes. It does not carry a per-deal cost, a filing fee, a
typical in-depth review duration in days, or a sector-by-sector breakdown beyond the manufacturing
share. Those numbers are not in the source material, so they are not in this article. If you need
them for a specific transaction, they have to come from the Commission's full report or from counsel,
not from an estimate here.

## AI Summary

## What happened

The European Commission published its sixth annual report on the screening of foreign direct investment into the EU, and its trade department summarised the findings on 14 October 2026.

The headline movement is in volume. Notifications to the EU's cooperation mechanism increased by 40% between 2024 and 2025. In 2025, EU Member States notified 667 investments to the Commission, up from 477 notifications in 2024.

The second movement is in depth. Of the 667 cases notified, 88% were closed within 15 days. The other 12% of the investments notified to the Commission required an in-depth security risk assessment — a 4% rise compared to last year.

## Why now

Two things make this year's report more than a statistical update.

First, the composition of the caseload has shifted toward the sector where reviews bite. Most such cases were in manufacturing, which accounted for 53% of all transactions, up from 50% in 2024. A larger share of a larger pile of notifications is landing in the sector that generates in-depth assessments.

Second, the legal basis is about to change. The EU's new Foreign Investment Screening Regulation (FISR) was adopted on 17 June 2026 and will apply from 17 January 2028. The figures in this report describe the regime that is running now, not the one that will be running after that date.

## So what

For anyone notifying a deal, the practical shape of the process is now two-track, and the report gives the split.

> "Of the 667 cases notified, 88% were closed within 15 days."
> — European Commission, sixth annual FDI screening report, 14 October 2026

That sentence is the base case. The complement of it is the planning problem: 12% of notified investments went to in-depth assessment, and the report does not state how long those took. What it does state is where they concentrated — manufacturing, at 53% of all transactions.

## How confident

High on the figures, limited on the consequences.

Every number in this article comes from the Commission's 14 October 2026 release and the sixth annual report it describes, and each is quoted in the source material behind this piece. The 40% increase, the 667 and 477 notification counts, the 88% and 12% splits, the 53% manufacturing share and the 17 January 2028 application date are all stated directly.

What the source material does not carry: a filing fee, a per-deal cost, the average duration of an in-depth assessment in days, or a sector breakdown beyond manufacturing. Those are not estimated here. Where this article says an in-depth review is a planning problem, that is an inference from the 12% share and the absence of a stated duration — not a figure.

## For you

- **Importers whose EU acquisition or greenfield stake is notifiable:** treat 15 days as the base case and hold contingency for the 12% that go to in-depth assessment, because the report gives no duration for that track.
- **Buyers targeting manufacturing assets:** assume in-depth review until told otherwise — manufacturing was 53% of all transactions in the notified population, and the Commission reports most in-depth cases were there.
- **Investors with a deal that could slip into 2028:** check the notification date against 17 January 2028, when FISR applies, because a deal assessed either side of that date runs under a different regulation.
- **Anyone modelling deal cost from this report alone:** do not. It carries no fee and no per-deal cost, so the cost of screening has to come from the full report or from counsel.

## The data point

| Measure | 2024 | 2025 | Change |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Investments notified to the Commission | 477 | 667 | +40% |
| Share closed within 15 days | not stated | 88% | — |
| Share requiring in-depth assessment | not stated | 12% | +4% on the year |
| Manufacturing share of all transactions | 50% | 53% | +3 points |

The 2024 column is thin because the release states only the 477 notification count and the 50% manufacturing share for that year. The 15-day and in-depth splits are given for 2025 only, and are shown as not stated rather than back-filled.

## FAQ

**How many EU investments were notified in 2025?**

EU Member States notified 667 investments to the Commission in 2025, up from 477 notifications in 2024. That is the 40% increase the Commission reports between the two years. The count is of investments notified to the Commission through the EU cooperation mechanism, not of every foreign investment made in the EU — Member States screen nationally as well, and this figure covers the cases that reached the EU level. For an investor, the number to take away is the direction of travel: the population of deals that get looked at is growing, so the odds that yours is among them are rising rather than falling.

**What share of notified deals closed within 15 days?**

Of the 667 cases notified, 88% were closed within 15 days. That is the clear majority and it is the base case to plan a completion timetable around. The remaining 12% did not clear in that window: 12% of the investments notified to the Commission required an in-depth security risk assessment, a 4% rise compared to last year. The report does not state how long an in-depth assessment takes, so the 12% should be treated as an open-ended contingency rather than a fixed extension of the 15-day clock.

**Which sector carries the in-depth reviews?**

Manufacturing. Most such cases were in manufacturing, which accounted for 53% of all transactions, up from 50% in 2024. Two things are happening at once in that sentence: manufacturing is a larger share of the notified population than it was, and it is where the Commission says the in-depth cases concentrate. For a buyer of a manufacturing asset, the 12% in-depth rate is not a portfolio average to be spread across sectors — it is the rate that applies most directly to the deal in front of you.

**When does the new screening regulation apply?**

The EU's new Foreign Investment Screening Regulation (FISR) was adopted on 17 June 2026 and will apply from 17 January 2028. Until that date, notifications run under the cooperation mechanism whose 2025 results are described in this report. The date matters for transaction timing: a deal notified before 17 January 2028 and one notified after it are assessed under different rules, so a completion timetable that crosses that date should be reviewed rather than assumed to carry over unchanged.

## How we calculated this

Nothing here is a calculation. Every figure is quoted from the European Commission's 14 October 2026 release on FDI screening and the sixth annual report it summarises, and each was checked against the archived source document before publication.

The one derived statement is the 40% increase, which the Commission states directly rather than leaving to be computed: notifications increased by 40% between 2024 and 2025, and the underlying counts are 477 and 667. The 4% rise in in-depth assessments is likewise the Commission's own wording.

The comparison table shows 2024 as "not stated" for the 15-day and in-depth splits because the release gives those shares for 2025 only. No figure has been back-filled, interpolated or estimated. Where the article draws a consequence — that an in-depth review is a planning problem, that manufacturing buyers should assume review — that is reasoning from the stated shares, and it is labelled as such in the confidence section.

## The point

The EU screened 667 notified investments in 2025, 40% more than the year before, and sent 12% of them into in-depth security review. Most of that review landed in manufacturing, which is now 53% of all transactions. The 15-day clearance that 88% of deals enjoy is real, but it is a base case, not a promise, and the report gives no duration for the track the other 12% are on. If you are buying into Europe, the number to carry into your timetable is the 12%, and the date to carry into your calendar is 17 January 2028.

- **Buyers targeting manufacturing assets:** assume in-depth review until told otherwise — manufacturing was 53% of all transactions in the notified population, and the Commission reports most in-depth cases were there.
- **Investors with a deal that can slip into 2028:** check the notification date against 17 January 2028, when FISR applies, because a deal assessed either side of that date runs under a different regulation.
- **Anyone modelling deal cost from this report alone:** do not. It carries no fee and no per-deal cost, so the cost of screening has to come from the full report or from counsel.

## The data point

| Measure | 2024 | 2025 | Change |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Investments notified to the Commission | 477 | 667 | +40% |
| Share closed within 15 days | not stated | 88% | — |
| Share requiring in-depth assessment | not stated | 12% | +4% on the year |
| Manufacturing share of all transactions | 50% | 53% | +3 points |

The 2024 column is thin because the release states only the 477 notification count and the 50% manufacturing share for that year. The 15-day and in-depth splits are given for 2025 only, and are shown as not stated rather than back-filled.

## FAQ

**How many EU investments were notified in 2025?**

EU Member States notified 667 investments to the Commission in 2025, up from 477 notifications in 2024. That is the 40% increase the Commission reports between the two years. The count is of investments notified to the Commission through the EU cooperation mechanism, not of every foreign investment made in the EU — Member States screen nationally as well, and this figure covers the cases that reached the EU level. For an investor, the number to take away is the direction of travel: the population of deals that get looked at is growing, so the odds that yours is among them are rising rather than falling.

**What share of notified deals closed within 15 days?**

Of the 667 cases notified, 88% were closed within 15 days. That is the clear majority and it is the base case to plan a completion timetable around. The remaining 12% did not clear in that window: 12% of the investments notified to the Commission required an in-depth security risk assessment, a 4% rise compared to last year. The report does not state how long an in-depth assessment takes, so the 12% should be treated as an open-ended contingency rather than a fixed extension of the 15-day clock.

**Which sector carries the in-depth reviews?**

Manufacturing. Most such cases were in manufacturing, which accounted for 53% of all transactions, up from 50% in 2024. Two things are happening at once in that sentence: manufacturing is a larger share of the notified population than it was, and it is where the Commission says the in-depth cases concentrate. For a buyer of a manufacturing asset, the 12% in-depth rate is not a portfolio average to be spread across sectors — it is the rate that applies most directly to the deal in front of you.

**When does the new screening regulation apply?**

The EU's new Foreign Investment Screening Regulation (FISR) was adopted on 17 June 2026 and will apply from 17 January 2028. Until that date, notifications run under the cooperation mechanism whose 2025 results are described in this report. The date matters for transaction timing: a deal notified before 17 January 2028 and one notified after it are assessed under different rules, so a completion timetable that crosses that date should be reviewed rather than assumed to carry over unchanged.

## How we calculated this

Nothing here is a calculation. Every figure is quoted from the European Commission's 14 October 2026 release on FDI screening and the sixth annual report it summarises, and each was checked against the archived source document before publication.

The one derived statement is the 40% increase, which the Commission states directly rather than leaving to be computed: notifications increased by 40% between 2024 and 2025, and the underlying counts are 477 and 667. The 4% rise in in-depth assessments is likewise the Commission's own wording.

The comparison table shows 2024 as "not stated" for the 15-day and in-depth splits because the release gives those shares for 2025 only. No figure has been back-filled, interpolated or estimated. Where the article draws a consequence — that an in-depth review is a planning problem, that manufacturing buyers should assume review — that is reasoning from the stated shares, and it is labelled as such in the confidence section.

## The point

The EU screened 667 notified investments in 2025, 40% more than the year before, and sent 12% of them into in-depth security review. Most of that review landed in manufacturing, which is now 53% of all transactions. The 15-day clearance that 88% of deals enjoy is real, but it is a base case, not a promise, and the report gives no duration for the track the other 12% are on. If you are buying into Europe, the number to carry into your timetable is the 12%, and the date to carry into your calendar is 17 January 2028.
